summary: Documents a number of popular extensions to the Network News Transfer Protocol that go beyond RFC 977. It is not a standard but a reference for implementers.

plainLanguage.summary: Usenet servers added extra commands over time. This writes down the popular ones so programmers can match them.

questions: what is the nntp xover command
subtitle: A catalogue of the extra NNTP commands that servers and newsreaders already used in 2000, written down for implementers.

tldr.problem: NNTP, defined in RFC 977, had grown many unofficial extra commands in server and newsreader software, and implementers had no single place that described them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC documents these extensions in three groups (transport, newsreader and other), gives each command's syntax and response codes, and notes where it first appeared and which are best treated as historic.
tldr.outcome: It is Informational and not a standard of any kind, and RFC 977 stays authoritative. Later RFCs have updated it.

today: RFC 2980 is an Informational RFC from October 2000 and was never a standard. It has been updated by RFC 3977, RFC 4643, RFC 4644 and RFC 6048.

sections.title: Why Document the Extensions
sections.content:
RFC 2980 documents popular extensions to the Network News Transfer Protocol (NNTP) defined in RFC 977. Work on a revised NNTP began in 1991 without producing a new standard, but many of its ideas, and many ideas from newsreader authors, ended up in software. The RFC captures the known extensions in official NNTP server releases as of its writing and notes which software first implemented each one.

It is explicit that it does not specify a standard. It documents current practice, RFC 977 is authoritative in all cases, and some listed commands should not be put in new implementations and are marked as historic. The extensions fall into three categories: transport (moving articles between servers), newsreader (helping clients select and fetch articles) and other, such as authentication and time of day.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a list of extra moves that news programs learned over time. The writers say it is only a guide, and the original rulebook still wins.

sections.title: Transport Extensions
sections.content:
Four commands move articles between servers faster than the lock-step style of RFC 977. MODE STREAM asks the server to suspend that lock-step conversation so commands can be sent in a stream; the server answers 203 if streaming is fine. CHECK <message-id> asks whether an article is wanted, and the sender does not have to wait for the answer before the next command. 238 means send it, while 438 means the server already has it and 431 means try again later.

TAKETHIS <message-id> is followed immediately by the whole article, header and body, and is answered with 239 on success or 439 on failure. Using CHECK is optional, and some implementations send TAKETHIS directly for everything in the queue.

XREPLIC first appeared in INN and lets one server duplicate the news spool layout of another by naming newsgroup and article number pairs. It should be used only when the receiving server has a single feed, and it has been deprecated in INN version 1.7.2 and later.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of asking for one package, waiting, then asking for the next, you can shout a whole list of requests and hand over the packages as the answers come back.

sections.title: Newsreader Extensions
sections.content:
This is the largest group. Several are LIST variants that expose files a news system already keeps: LIST ACTIVE, LIST ACTIVE.TIMES, LIST DISTRIBUTIONS, LIST DISTRIB.PATS, LIST NEWSGROUPS, LIST OVERVIEW.FMT and LIST SUBSCRIPTIONS. The RFC recommends adding LIST subcommands rather than new verbs, for example LIST MOTD instead of XMOTD.

Other commands include LISTGROUP (all article numbers in a group), MODE READER (the client says it is a reader), XHDR (one header from many articles), XOVER (overview data, as tab-separated fields in the order subject, author, date, message-id, references, byte count, line count), XPAT (header search by pattern), XPATH, XROVER, XGTITLE, XINDEX and XTHREAD.

The RFC advises that XGTITLE be deprecated because it duplicates LIST NEWSGROUPS, and recommends that XINDEX and XTHREAD become historic because newsreaders moved to the overview format. It says LIST OVERVIEW.FMT is strongly recommended wherever XOVER is implemented. Patterns for choosing newsgroups use the wildmat format, which supports an asterisk for any run of characters, a question mark for any single character, character sets in square brackets, negated sets and backslash escapes. It is not a regular expression language.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the shortcuts a news reader uses to ask the server for a list of groups, a list of headlines, or a search, without downloading every article.

sections.title: AUTHINFO, DATE and Added Headers
sections.content:
AUTHINFO identifies the user to the server, and clients must supply it when the server asks. The original form uses AUTHINFO USER and AUTHINFO PASS: the server sends 480, the client sends the user name, the server may reply 381 to ask for a password, and 281 means accepted, after which the client retries the original command. A bad combination gets 502. Everything travels in cleartext.

AUTHINFO SIMPLE came from the NNTP version 2 proposal that was never completed. It uses response codes that violate RFC 977, and the RFC recommends not implementing it. AUTHINFO GENERIC hands the exchange to a named authentication protocol, similar to those in RFC 1731 for IMAP4. After authentication the server generates a Sender: line if the authenticated address differs from From:.

DATE returns 111 followed by the server's GMT time as YYYYMMDDhhmmss. Servers also add headers such as NNTP-Posting-Host to posted articles, and the RFC says reverse DNS lookups used for it are not foolproof.
sections.plainLanguage: AUTHINFO is the news server asking for your name and password at the door. Some versions of the door knock were sent in plain sight, so anyone watching could read your password.

sections.title: Common Implementation Issues
sections.content:
Section 4 records where real servers depart from RFC 977. The fourth field of the LIST reply often has more values than y or n, because most servers print the active file as is. Modern servers require only From, Subject and Newsgroups in a posted article and supply the rest, and many implementers think clients should generate as few headers as possible.

Article numbers only increase and articles may disappear, so the high and low marks from GROUP should be read as bounds, not exact counts. Some servers let administrators disable RFC 977 commands, and NEWNEWS is often disabled, so clients cannot depend on every command. For NEWNEWS with a distributions argument, some servers match the Distribution header while others match newsgroup name prefixes, a split that traces back to RFC 1036 changing how distribution works.
sections.plainLanguage: This part is a list of the ways real news servers bend the original rules, so programmers know not to be surprised.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The only security discussion concerns AUTHINFO, which is optional. In the original and simple forms, passwords are sent in plaintext and can be found by network or system surveillance. AUTHINFO GENERIC has the same weakness if the mechanism it uses also sends cleartext passwords. RFC 1731 discusses these issues in more detail.
sections.plainLanguage: If you shout your password across a crowded room, anyone can hear it. Some of these login methods work that way.
